The Orlando Magic are an American professional basketball team based in Orlando, Florida.
The Orlando Magic compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member of the Southeast Division of the Eastern Conference.
The franchise was established in 1989 as an expansion franchise.
Shaquille O'Neal, Penny Hardaway, Grant Hill, Tracy McGrady, and Dwight Howard have played for the club throughout its history.
As of 2024[update], the franchise has played in the NBA playoffs 17 times in 35 seasons.
The Orlando Magic have twice gone to the NBA Finals, in 1995 and 2009.
In 1985–1986, Jim L. Hewitt approached Pat Williams of the Philadelphia 76ers about bringing an NBA team to Orlando.
In September 1985, Hewitt and Williams decided to hold a contest in the Orlando Sentinel newspaper for names for their new franchise.
Out of 4,296 submitted entries, "Magic" was chosen as the name after Williams' daughter Karyn suggested it.
The name "Magic" alludes to Walt Disney World's Magic Kingdom.
Hewitt brought investors such as William DuPont and Jim Caruso, and talked Orlando city officials into approving an arena project.
Williams gave presentations to NBA commissioner David Stern and other team owners about the viability of Orlando as a franchise location.
In April 1986, the franchise committee recommended expanding by three teams with two slots going to Charlotte and Minneapolis-St. Paul.
The recommendation put the Orlando bid in doubt since Florida was only allocated one team for expansion.
When both Miami and Orlando made successful pitches, the expansion committee decided to expand by four teams, allowing both to have a franchise.
The Magic became the first major-league professional sports franchise in the Orlando area with an expansion fee of $32.5 million.
They were one of the four new expansion franchises awarded by the NBA in 1987 along with Charlotte Hornets, Miami Heat, and Minnesota Timberwolves.
The Magic hired Matt Guokas as their first coach.
On June 15, 1989, the Magic selected 12 players in the NBA Expansion Draft.
On June 27, 1989, the Magic chose Nick Anderson with the 11th pick in the first round of the 1989 NBA Draft.
The Orlando Arena (O-Rena) was the home of the Magic from 1989 to 2010.
The Magic's very first game played was an exhibition match on October 13, 1989, against the Detroit Pistons.
On November 4, 1989, the Magic played their first season game at the Orlando Arena (O-Rena) against the New Jersey Nets.
In the 1989–1992 period, Dennis Scott set a team record with 125 three-point field goals for the season.
The DeVos family purchased the franchise for $85 million on September 19, 1991.
Richard DeVos became the owner of the franchise.
In the 1990 NBA draft, the Orlando Magic selected Dennis Scott with the fourth overall pick.
On December 30, 1990, Scott Skiles recorded a single-game record of 30 assists in a victory over the Denver Nuggets.
The Magic heralded the NBA's most improved record that season as Scott was named the NBA's Most Improved Player.
Dennis Scott set a team mark with 125 three-point field goals for the season.
He was named to the NBA All-Rookie First Team.
In the 1991–92 season, Dennis Scott played only 18 games due to injuries.
Nick Anderson missed 22 games in the same season.
Stanley Roberts, Jerry Reynolds, Brian Williams, Sam Vincent, and Otis Smith all missed at least 27 games each during that season.
The Magic struggled through a 17-game losing streak and finished with a 21–61 record for the 1991–92 season.
All 41 home games were sold out in the 1991–92 season.
In May 17, 1992, the Magic won the first pick in the 1992 NBA draft Lottery.
The Magic selected Shaquille O'Neal from Louisiana State University with that pick.
O'Neal led the team to a 41–41 record and became the first rookie to be voted an All-Star starter since Michael Jordan in 1985.
Despite O'Neal's presence, the Magic missed the 1993 NBA playoffs because they were tied with Indiana Pacers for the eighth and final playoff spot with the Pacers holding the tiebreaker.
In the 1992–93 season, the Orlando Magic selected Chris Webber in the first round of the 1993 NBA draft Lottery.
The Magic traded Chris Webber to the Golden State Warriors for Anfernee "Penny" Hardaway and three future first-round picks.
With O'Neal and Hardaway, the Magic became a dominant team in the NBA with their first 50-win season.
The Magic were seeded fourth in the Eastern Conference and ranked as the second-best all-time record of the Chicago Bulls.
In the playoffs, the Magic defeated the Boston Celtics, Bulls, and Indiana Pacers to advance to the NBA Finals where they lost to Hakeem Olajuwon and the Houston Rockets 4–0.
The Orlando Magic hired Chuck Daly as head coach for the 1997–98 season.
Julius Erving joined the Magic's front office in 1997–98, giving hope for a successful season.
In the 1998–99 season, Michael Doleac and Matt Harpring were selected with the 12th and 15th picks of the 1998 NBA draft.
Penny Hardaway led the Magic to tie for the Eastern Conference's best record in a lockout-shortened season.
Darrell Armstrong was a constant leader on the Orlando Magic team, leading from the vanguard.
Armstrong won the NBA Sixth-Man and Most Improved Player awards during his tenure with the Magic.
Dominique Wilkins and his brother were acquired by the Magic but their careers had declined.
In 1998–99, the Orlando Magic's slogan was "Heart and Hustle".
The Orlando Magic hired rookie-coach Doc Rivers in 1999.
Doc Rivers led the Magic to a 41–41 record with a team composed of no-name players and little experience.
At the end of the season, Rivers was named Coach of the Year.

In the off-season following the 2003–04 season, general manager John Gabriel dismantled the previous team by trading Penny Hardaway to the Phoenix Suns for Danny Manning, Pat Garrity, and two future draft picks.
The Magic were a team composed of virtually all no-name players and little experience in 1999.
In the 2000–2004 period, the Orlando Magic acquired Tracy McGrady from the San Antonio Spurs.
Tracy McGrady led the Magic to a winning record of 44–38 during the 2001–02 season.
Grant Hill was severely limited by his ankle injury and did not play for most of the 2001–02 season.
In 2002–03, McGrady led the Magic to a 42–40 record with Armstrong, Miller, and Pat Garrity as key players.
McGrady made the All-NBA First Team and Third All-Star Team in 2002–03.
The Magic entered the playoffs for the third straight year but lost to Detroit Pistons 4–3 after taking a 3–1 lead.
In 2003–04, the Orlando Magic struggled early with Tyronn Lue and Juwan Howard as key players.
After winning their first game, the Magic lost 19 consecutive games setting a franchise record.
The Magic finished an NBA worst 21–61 in the 2003–04 season.
Despite this, McGrady led the league in scoring with 28.0 points per game and made his fourth consecutive All-Star Team.
Coach Doc Rivers was fired mid-season after leading Davis to believe he would be the team's head coach for the entire 2004–05 NBA season.
Assistant Johnny Davis was promoted to head coach.
General manager Gabriel was replaced by John Weisbrod.
Dwight Howard was drafted No. 1 overall in the 2004 NBA draft.
Weisbrod completely dismantled the team, keeping only a few players from last season.
The Magic traded McGrady along with Reece Gaines, Tyronn Lue, and Juwan Howard to the Houston Rockets for Steve Francis, Kelvin Cato, and Cuttino Mobley.
In addition, the Magic acquired center Tony Battie and two second-round draft picks from the Cleveland Cavaliers in exchange for Drew Gooden, Steven Hunter, and the draft rights to Anderson Varejão.
The Magic signed free agent Hedo Türkoğlu.
With the number one draft pick, the Magic selected high-school phenomenon Dwight Howard and a point guard Jameer Nelson.
After a promising 13–6 start, the Magic began to fall apart with Doug Christie's refusal to play for the Magic after emotional ties to the Kings.
Near the end of the season, with a playoff-push faltering, Weisbrod fired Davis and promoted Chris Jent as interim head coach.
The Magic finished the 2004–05 season 36–46.
Hedo Türkoğlu was sidelined by a broken wrist in the final quarter of the season.
Grant Hill suffered a shin injury that limited his play throughout the season.
Nelson had a rib cage injury and was suspended for three games due to kicking a photographer.
The Magic ended a few games out of the playoffs.
On May 23, 2005, general manager John Weisbrod resigned abruptly.
Brian Hill returned as head coach on October 21 after leading the team to the NBA Finals under O'Neal and Hardaway.
The Orlando Magic drafted Spanish Fran Vázquez with the 11th pick in the 2005 NBA draft.
On July 28, 2005, Vazquez announced he would remain in Spain to play for Akasvayu Girona.
Owner Rich DeVos announced on October 21 that he was transferring ownership to his children with Bob Vander Weide as team president.
The transfer was supposed to be complete by the end of the year.
The 2005–06 season opened with high hopes for the Magic despite not being able to add first-round draft pick Vasquez.
Grant Hill, despite ankle surgeries, suffered a painful sports hernia injury that hampered his play throughout the entire season.
After playing in three preseason games, he underwent surgery and did not appear until mid-December.
Hill played sporadically after attempting another comeback in February and early March but only played for a month.
A foot injury to Jameer Nelson forced him to sit out for over a month.
On February 15, the Magic acquired Darko Miličić and Carlos Arroyo from the Detroit Pistons in exchange for Kelvin Cato and a 2007 top-five protected first-round draft pick.
One week later, Steve Francis was traded to the New York Knicks in exchange for Penny Hardaway (waived two days later) and Trevor Ariza.
With a set starting rotation of Battie, Howard, Türkoğlu, DeShawn Stevenson, and Nelson, the Magic mounted an unexpected run at the eighth playoff spot with 12 consecutive home wins.
Despite their efforts, they did not make the playoffs.
Head coach Stan Van Gundy signed a five-year contract on June 1, 2007.
On June 6, 2007, Billy Donovan was released from his contract and Stan Van Gundy signed a four-year deal with the Magic.
In the free agent market, the Magic signed Rashard Lewis to a six-year league-maximum contract worth over $110 million.
The Magic swept the three games in China against the Cleveland Cavaliers and Chinese national team during the NBA China Games.
Bob Vander Weide officially took over as owner of the team on November 15, 2007.
The Orlando Magic started the 2007–08 season with an impressive 16–4 record in their first 20 games.
Through the next few months, they split their next 36 games with 18 wins and 18 losses.
At the start of March, the Magic finished the month with 10 wins, the first time since November that they won 10 or more in a month.
The Magic clinched the Southeast Division title on March 31, 2008.
They also earned their 50th win of the season against the Chicago Bulls on April 13, which had not happened since the 1995–96 season.
With the third seed in the Eastern Conference, they were matched up in their first-round playoff series against the Toronto Raptors.
The Magic won the first round with a 4–1 series victory over the Raptors.
They fell to the Detroit Pistons 4–1 in the second round despite being down in the series.
On April 28, 2008, the Magic eliminated the Raptors with a 4–1 series victory in the first round of the playoffs.
The run of success did not last long as they were swept by the Detroit Pistons in the second round.
In the 2009 off-season, Orlando traded Rafer Alston, Tony Battie, and Courtney Lee to the New Jersey Nets for Vince Carter and Ryan Anderson.
Hedo Türkoğlu was sent to the Toronto Raptors via a sign-and-trade deal.
The Magic signed Brandon Bass, Matt Barnes, and Jason Williams as free agents.
On September 28, 2009, head coach Stan Van Gundy's contract was extended by exercising his option for the 2010–11 season.
General manager Otis Smith's contract was also extended through the 2011–12 season.
The Magic were without Rashard Lewis for the first 10 games of the 2009–10 season due to a banned substance in an over-the-counter supplement.
Vince Carter suffered a left ankle injury in just the second game of the season and missed five games.
Jameer Nelson injured his left knee, which required arthroscopic surgery to repair, and was out for five weeks.
Despite all this, the Magic had a 23–8 record at the end of December.
The Magic lost seven of their first ten games in January but recovered well enough to post a winning record by winning six of their next seven.
Following the All-Star break, they won 23 of their 28 remaining games and clinched their fourth consecutive playoff berth.
They also won their third consecutive division championship.
The Magic finished the regular season with a 59–23 record, matching their record from the 2008–09 season.
They became one of only teams in NBA history to beat all other 29 teams at least once during the regular season.
The Magic swept the Charlotte Bobcats and Atlanta Hawks in the first two rounds of the playoffs.
In the conference finals, they faced the Boston Celtics but lost after dropping the first three games and winning the next two before losing Game 6.
Scott Skiles coached the Orlando Magic in the 2015–16 season.
The Magic updated their logo to feature a streaking ball with stars for the new Amway Center.
The Magic hosted the NBA All-Star Game in 2012.
In December 2010, the Magic made a blockbuster trade deal with Phoenix Suns and Washington Wizards.
They traded Vince Carter, Marcin Gortat, and Jason Richardson to Phoenix for Hedo Türkoğlu, Earl Clark, and Jason Richardson.
Rashard Lewis was traded to Washington for Gilbert Arenas.
The Magic finished the season with 52 victories, good for second in the Southeast Division.
But they were eliminated by the Atlanta Hawks in six games in the first round of the 2011 NBA playoffs.
In a lockout-shortened 2011–12 season, Dwight Howard requested a trade to either New Jersey Nets, Los Angeles Lakers, or Dallas Mavericks.
The Magic traded Glen Davis and Von Wafer to Boston for Brandon Bass.
They also amnestied Gilbert Arenas and signed Larry Hughes, Justin Harper, and DeAndre Liggins.
